paras: The Portsmouth lynching threats of 1903 were threats of mob violence in July 1903 against George Washington Griggs, a young Black man held in the jail at Portsmouth, Virginia, on a charge of assaulting the four-year-old daughter of a Port Norfolk dairyman. A group of men from Port Norfolk came to the jail soon after his arrest, but the sheriff's armed guard kept the prisoner and no violence followed. Griggs was convicted and sentenced to eighteen years in the penitentiary, and a Richmond paper reported that lynching had also been threatened against John Edwards, a Black man tried in the same court for assaulting an eleven-year-old Black girl.

Griggs, called "George Washington" in the first reports, worked for Isaac B. Mason, "the Port Norfolk dairyman." According to the Alexandria Gazette, the alleged attack on the Masons' four-year-old daughter took place the previous Thursday while the family was away and was not discovered until Sunday; a later Richmond dispatch dated it July 3. In a report printed on July 7, the Gazette said he had been arrested "yesterday morning" and lodged in the Portsmouth jail.

Rumors spread that an attempt would be made to lynch the prisoner, and Sheriff Cromwell kept the county jail guarded overnight with "a large force of officers heavily armed." According to the Alexandria Gazette, "a small group of indignant men from Port Norfolk" appeared at the jail very early in the morning and demanded that the jailer surrender the prisoner. The jailer refused and sent for reinforcements, and the men then moved off "to avoid arrest," the paper said.

The Washington Times put the group at about a dozen men from Port Norfolk, "the home of the victim," and said they "made no hostile demonstration," while the Evening Star reported that no attack on the jail was attempted. The guards were doubled, and the Washington Times found "great indignation at Port Norfolk" but little fear of an attack, since nobody doubted that the accused would have an early trial.

Griggs went on trial in Portsmouth on July 27, where, according to the Times-Dispatch's Norfolk correspondent, the child identified him and told her story "in an intelligible and direct manner." The same dispatch recalled an "intimation of lynching" after the arrest but saw no sign of dissatisfaction with the probable result of the trial. His punishment was fixed on July 27 at eighteen years in the penitentiary, and he asked for a new trial. Judge Portlock formally sentenced him to that term on August 4.

The July 28 dispatch also reported that John Edwards, "colored," was on trial in the same court for a criminal assault on Ada Wright, an eleven-year-old Black girl. It added that "there were threats of lynching for both of these negroes, but the promise of speedy trials averted violence." No other account of threats against Edwards, and no report of the verdict in his case, appears in the coverage.

The case was reported in white newspapers in Virginia and Washington; no Black-press account of it appears in the coverage. The Alexandria Gazette headlined its jail story "Lynchers Frustrated," called the men "would-be avengers of the crime," and ran it alongside a story of a South Carolina sheriff's daughter who turned away a lynch mob with a rifle. The Evening Star's brief special dispatch, "Lynching Feared at Portsmouth," centered on the sheriff's precautions.

The Richmond Times-Dispatch carried the case in its Norfolk correspondent's columns among court, shipping and society items, under headlines such as "Mulatto in Portsmouth Being Tried on Serious Charge" and "Negro Gets Eighteen Years." Its later reports treated the assault as established: the July 29 headline spoke of the "Negro Who Assaulted Four-Year-Old Child," and the sentencing item called it "a particularly vicious assault" while noting that "the officers protected the negro."

The papers named the girl's father as Isaac B. Mason, Bruce Mason or John Mason, and the child as Marie, Maria or Marion. Early reports described an attempted assault; the trial reports, a criminal assault. Accounts also differed on what happened at the jail: the Gazette described a demand for the prisoner, while the Washington Times and the Evening Star reported no hostile demonstration and no attack.
